title: Enuresis before university
question: A 17-year-old adolescent about to commence university has persistent enuresis. Discuss a proposed management plan with the mother.
modelAnswer: Acknowledge embarrassment and explore the young personâ€™s goals. Involve the adolescent, seek permission to discuss with the mother and offer private conversation. Explain that wetting is involuntary; avoid blame. Clarify lifelong wetting versus recurrence after six dry months; ask about daytime symptoms, constipation, urinary infection, thirst, weight loss, snoring and psychosocial stress. Use a bladder/bowel diary and focused examination. Investigate red flags; do not order routine imaging for uncomplicated primary enuresis. Address constipation and daytime symptoms. Encourage normal daytime drinking, regular toileting and voiding before bed; reward helpful behaviours. Agree a practical university plan for privacy, laundry and follow-up. Offer an alarm when acceptable and feasible. Consider oral desmopressin when rapid short-term dryness matters or an alarm is unsuitable. Explain relapse and fluid restriction from one hour before until eight hours after the dose; avoid use when restriction cannot be followed. Discuss hyponatraemia symptoms and urgent assessment for severe headache, vomiting, confusion or seizures. Review response at four weeks. Refer for red flags or failure of alarm/desmopressin treatment. Check understanding and agree the next appointment.
role: Play the mother. Ask whether this is laziness, whether an alarm will disturb roommates, and what can help before university. Reveal no additional symptoms unless asked; do not invent test results. End with the adolescentâ€™s preferences and a shared plan.
checklist: Involve adolescent; discuss privacy and consent
Screen constipation and medical red flags
Discuss fluids, toileting and positive reinforcement
Explain desmopressin fluid restriction and safety
Plan university privacy and practical support
critical: Do not give desmopressin without fluid-safety counselling
Escalate suspected diabetes or neurological disease

stations.title: Practice consultation
stations.brief: Discuss a management plan with the relative.
stations.role: A concerned relative in a simulated station.

phases.title: Open and seek permission
phases.action: Introduce yourself and check permission to discuss the plan
phases.say: Hello, I am the doctor. May we discuss the plan together?
phases.expect: Can I stay for this discussion?
phases.reply: Let us check what the patient wants shared with you.
phases.reason: Establish consent and the patient’s preferences.

phases.title: Explore concerns
phases.action: Ask what worries the patient and relative most
phases.say: What concerns you most about the current situation?
phases.expect: I am worried about the next term.
phases.reply: Tell me which parts of the move concern you.

phases.title: Agree a plan
phases.action: Explain the sourced options and agree a plan
phases.say: Let us compare the options and decide what fits your goals.
phases.reply: We can discuss the benefits and practical issues together.

phases.title: Close and check understanding
phases.say: Could you explain the agreed next steps in your own words?
phases.reply: Let us arrange a review and discuss when to seek help sooner.
phases.reason: Check understanding and make follow-up clear.
